intro: ね, よ and よね go at the very end of a sentence and say who holds the information. ね says "we both have this": you expect the listener to know or feel the same, so you invite agreement. よ says "I have this and you don't": you are handing the listener something new. よね joins the two: "I believe this, and I expect you to confirm it." Before you choose, ask whose head the information is already in.

skills.rule: End with ね when the listener already knows or feels the same thing and you want them to agree: "isn't it?", "right?".
skills.explain:
ね puts the statement on common ground. Use it for things you both experience at the same moment (いい天気ですね, this food is good, that was tiring), for sympathy (大変でしたね), and for checking a detail the listener has just told you or that you both know (三時ですね). Said with a falling tone it shares a feeling; with a slight rise it asks for a nod.

The edge is new information. If the listener cannot know what you are saying, ね sounds as though you are telling them their own business. Your own birthday, news they missed, or a fact only you saw takes よ or no particle, not ね. One exception: a hesitant answer (えーと、五月ですね) uses ね to think aloud.

In plain speech ね follows verbs and い-adjectives directly (寒いね, 行くね), and a noun or な-adjective takes だ first: 静かだね, 日曜日だね. ね is also used to soften a request or mark your own decision lightly (じゃ、また明日ね).
patterns: [detail you both know] ですね  "that's right, isn't it?"

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は暑[あつ]いです{ね}。
このケーキ、おいしい{ね}。
examples.en: This cake is good, isn't it?

examples.jp: きれいな花[はな]です{ね}。
昨日[きのう]は大変[たいへん]でした{ね}。
examples.en: Yesterday must have been hard for you.

examples.jp: じゃ、会議[かいぎ]は三時[さんじ]からです{ね}。
examples.en: So the meeting starts at three, right?

examples.jp: この辺[へん]は静[しず]かだ{ね}。
examples.en: It's quiet around here, isn't it?

contrast.note: よ hands over information the listener lacks; ね appeals to information or feelings you share. Both of you looking at the rain: 雨ですね. Telling someone indoors that it has started raining: 雨ですよ.
か asks a real question with no expectation: 暑いですか (Are you hot?). ね expects a yes: 暑いですね (Hot, isn't it?).

mistakes.bad: （友達[ともだち]が気[き]づいていない）後[うし]ろから車[くるま]が来[き]ています{ね}。
mistakes.good: （友達[ともだち]が気[き]づいていない）後[うし]ろから車[くるま]が来[き]ています{よ}。
mistakes.note: Your friend has not seen the car. A warning is new information and takes よ; ね would assume they had already noticed.

mistakes.bad: さっき田中[たなか]さんから電話[でんわ]がありました{ね}。
mistakes.good: さっき田中[たなか]さんから電話[でんわ]がありました{よ}。
mistakes.note: Passing on a message the listener missed is new information: よ, not ね.

skills.tip: Could the listener nod and say "yes, I know" or "yes, I feel that too"? Then ね.

skills.rule: End with よ when you are telling the listener something they don't know or haven't noticed: "I'm telling you", "you know".
skills.explain:
よ marks the sentence as new to the listener. Use it to inform (バスが来ましたよ), to warn (危ないですよ), to recommend (この本、面白いですよ), to correct (違いますよ), and to answer a question with some force (大丈夫ですよ, "it's fine, really"). It also strengthens suggestions and requests: 行きましょうよ, 待ってよ.

The edge is shared information. Telling someone what they can see or feel themselves, such as the weather you are both standing in, sounds like a lecture; use ね there. Overused, よ turns pushy: to a superior, 違いますよ can sound like you are correcting them sharply, so keep it for help and reassurance.

In plain speech よ follows verbs and い-adjectives directly (行くよ, 高いよ), and a noun or な-adjective takes だ first: 学生だよ, 元気だよ. Women's speech can drop だ (学生よ), but that is a style choice, not the neutral form.
patterns: [new information] よ  "you know / I'm telling you"
[let's / please] ましょうよ / てよ  "come on"

examples.jp: その道[みち]は危[あぶ]ないです{よ}。
examples.en: That road is dangerous, you know.

examples.jp: この映画[えいが]、すごく面白[おもしろ]い{よ}。
examples.en: This film is really good, I promise.

examples.jp: 大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]です{よ}。心配[しんぱい]しないでください。
一緒[いっしょ]に行[い]きましょう{よ}。

contrast.note: ね assumes the listener already shares the information; よ assumes they don't. Your friend has spinach on their tooth: you say 歯に何か付いてるよ, never ね.
か asks; よ tells. 明日休みですか: Is tomorrow a day off? 明日休みですよ: Tomorrow is a day off, just so you know.

mistakes.bad: （二人[ふたり]で空[そら]を見[み]て）きれいな空[そら]です{よ}。
mistakes.good: （二人[ふたり]で空[そら]を見[み]て）きれいな空[そら]です{ね}。
mistakes.note: You are both looking at the same sky; there is nothing new to hand over. Shared impressions take ね.

mistakes.bad: （二人[ふたり]で同[おな]じ料理[りょうり]を食[た]べて）おいしいです{よ}。
mistakes.good: （二人[ふたり]で同[おな]じ料理[りょうり]を食[た]べて）おいしいです{ね}。
mistakes.note: You are both tasting the same dish, so the taste is shared. よ fits before the listener tries it: "it's good, you'll see".

skills.tip: Would "just so you know" fit in English? Then よ.

skills.rule: End with よね when you are fairly sure of something and want the listener to confirm it: "..., right?", "didn't you?".
skills.explain:
よね is よ followed by ね, always in that order. The よ part says "this is my belief", the ね part says "you will agree". The result is a check: you are not asking from zero, and you are not sharing an obvious feeling; you are testing your memory or assumption against the listener's. 明日は休みですよね: Tomorrow's a day off, isn't it? (I think so; tell me I'm right.)

Compare the three ways to say it. 明日は休みですか asks with no expectation. 明日は休みですね agrees with something both of you know, or repeats what you have just been told. 明日は休みですよね checks your own belief. When you remember something but are not certain, よね is the natural choice.

よね also states opinions you expect to be shared (この歌、いいよね, "this song is great, don't you think?"). In plain speech a noun or な-adjective takes だ: 学生だよね. The reverse order ねよ does not exist.
patterns: [past fact you remember] ましたよね  "you did ..., didn't you?"

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は休[やす]みです{よね}。
田中[たなか]さんは大阪[おおさか]出身[しゅっしん]です{よね}。
examples.en: You're from Osaka, aren't you, Mr Tanaka?
This song is great, don't you think?

examples.jp: 鍵[かぎ]、ちゃんと閉[し]めた{よね}。
examples.en: You did lock the door, didn't you?

examples.jp: 会議[かいぎ]の資料[しりょう]はもう送[おく]りました{よね}。
examples.en: I've already sent you the meeting documents, haven't I?

contrast.note: ね agrees about something you both clearly know or feel; よね checks something you believe but want confirmed. Looking at the rain together: 雨だね. Thinking the forecast said rain: 明日は雨だよね.
か is an open question; よね leans towards yes. 山田さんは来ますか: Is Ms Yamada coming? 山田さんは来ますよね: Ms Yamada is coming, isn't she?
よ tells the listener something; よね asks them to confirm it. 宿題は明日までだよ: The homework is due tomorrow (I'm telling you). 宿題は明日までだよね: It's due tomorrow, right?

mistakes.bad: 試験[しけん]は来週[らいしゅう]です{ねよ}。
mistakes.good: 試験[しけん]は来週[らいしゅう]です{よね}。
mistakes.note: The order is fixed: よ then ね. ねよ is never used.

mistakes.bad: A：トイレはどこですか。B：二階[にかい]です{よね}。
mistakes.good: A：トイレはどこですか。B：二階[にかい]です{よ}。
mistakes.note: The listener asked because they don't know; asking them to confirm makes no sense. Answer with よ or plain です.

skills.tip: "I think so; am I right?" is よね. Say よ first, then ね, the order you think it.
